title: Answering the Other Side
subtitle: Evaluating how an argument handles a counterargument
subject: English language arts
objectives: Students will be able to identify an author's claim and the counterargument the author answers.
Students will be able to evaluate how well a rebuttal answers a counterargument, citing specific lines.
targets: I can find a writer's claim and the other side they answer.
I can judge how well a writer answers the other side, with evidence.
standards: CCSS RI.11-12.1: cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis
CCSS RI.11-12.6: determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text
CCSS W.11-12.1b: develop claims and counterclaims fairly

vocabulary.meaning: The position the writer argues for.
The other side: a reason someone would disagree. Also called a counterargument.
Admitting the other side has a point.
The writer's answer to the counterclaim.

sequence.teacher: Pose the question; take two or three answers and write the strongest on the board.

slides.title: Do now
slides.prompt: Someone disagrees with you. Is it stronger to ignore their point, or to admit it and answer it? Why?
slides.say: Steer toward: admitting a real point makes you more believable, if your answer holds up.

sequence.teacher: Teach the three moves for the other side and what makes a rebuttal strong, then model an evaluation on a different argument (phones in class).
sequence.students: Take notes; predict each step of the model.

slides.say: Counterclaim is the word on state tests; counterargument means the same thing.

slides.title: Three moves for the other side
points: **Name it** fairly: what would a critic say?
**Rebut**: show why your claim still holds, with evidence.
slides.callout: A rebuttal is only as strong as the evidence behind it.
slides.say: These are the writer's moves. Next: how a reader judges them.

slides.title: Strong or thin?
slides.say: Either verdict can be right: what matters is the evidence for it.

slides.title: A different argument
slides.text:
Our school should ban phones during class. Some parents worry they won't
reach their kids in an emergency. That's a fair worry. But the front office
phone works fine, and phones in class cost students hours of focus a week.
slides.focus: Name the counterclaim, the concession, and the rebuttal.
slides.say: Counterclaim: parents can't reach kids (lines 1-2). Concession: 'That's a fair worry.' Rebuttal: the office phone works (line 3).

slides.title: Judging a rebuttal
slides.problem: How well does the principal answer the parents' worry about emergencies?
steps: **Explain:** it doesn't say how a parent reaches a child in a lockdown, when the office is busiest.
slides.say: Pause before each step: ask what position the class would take, which words they'd cite, and what those words show.

sequence.teacher: Students find each move in a new short argument on whiteboards, then judge the rebuttal with a partner.
sequence.students: Answer on whiteboards, then talk with a partner.

slides.title: We do: find the concession
slides.prompt: "Homework takes family time. That's true. But practice builds skill." Which is the concession?
slides.why: "That's true" admits the other side's point; the next sentence rebuts it.
slides.answer_say: Then ask pairs: is this rebuttal strong or thin, and what would make it stronger?

sequence.teacher: Hand out the worksheet. Students read the op-ed and highlight the claim in one color and the counterclaim in the other; no questions yet.

sequence.then: Done? Write one sentence the author could add to make the rebuttal stronger.
sequence.teacher: Conference with two or three students on their position sentence. Collect every sheet when time's up.
sequence.students: Answer both questions on their own.
Answer on an index card, on their own.

slides.title: Exit ticket
slides.prompt: "Uniforms save families money, though some say they limit self-expression." What is the counterclaim?
slides.say: Cards that name 'saving money' have the claim and the counterclaim switched: start there tomorrow.

checks: What is the author's claim, in one sentence?
Which line concedes a point to critics?
Does the Seattle study answer the critics' worry?

misconceptions.misconception: Agreeing with the author means the rebuttal is strong.
misconceptions.response: Separate the two: you can agree with the claim and still find the answer to critics thin.

misconceptions.misconception: Summarizing the op-ed counts as evaluating it.
misconceptions.response: Ask for a judgment word: strong, partial, thin, convincing, and then why.

support: Give the sentence frame: "The author answers the critics ___ because ___ (line __)."
extension: Write the strongest version of the critics' argument, then answer it yourself.
language: Pair claim, concession, and rebuttal with icons on the vocabulary slide.
Allow a first draft in the student's first language before writing in English.

walkthrough.think: Which choice could every paragraph of the op-ed be supporting?
walkthrough.idea: A claim is what the whole piece argues for, not one detail in it.
steps: A is a fix the author rejects ("the problem isn't willpower").
C and D are pieces of the argument: a counterclaim and evidence.
B is what every paragraph builds toward.
mistakes: Picking D: Seattle's grades are evidence for the claim, not the claim.

walkthrough.think: Does the author show that sports and buses can be fixed, or just say so?
walkthrough.idea: Judge the rebuttal by its evidence: this one asserts more than it shows.
walkthrough.model: The author answers the critics only partly. The op-ed concedes that later start times have "real costs" (line 7) but calls them "problems of logistics" that "can be solved" (lines 7-8) without showing how. The Seattle results (lines 5-6) show that students slept more, not that buses and sports adjusted. The rebuttal would be convincing with one example of a district that solved the scheduling problems.
mistakes: Summarizing the op-ed instead of judging the rebuttal.
Quoting without explaining what the quote shows.
walkthrough.say: A paragraph that argues the rebuttal is strong earns full credit too, if it cites two lines and explains them.

assessment: A student who has it names the author's claim and the counterclaim, takes a clear position on how well the author answers it, and backs that position with at least two accurate citations and an explanation of what they show. A well-argued "strong" verdict earns full credit as much as a "thin" one.
